workflow.title: Writing an FCA report
workflow.description: How to build, write, and send a functional capacity assessment report in the portal, with clear, sourced and honest content that links each support to a goal and to reasonable and necessary criteria. Five interactive walkthroughs, including a live tour of the FCA template.

items.title: Walkthrough: Paint the picture
items.body:
**Start here.** What an FCA is for, the five NDIS domains, and why an honest report the planner can trust beats a dramatic one.

Your place is saved if you stop part-way.

items.title: Walkthrough: Build the evidence
items.body: Tailor the report to the disability, name every source, and choose each assessment for a reason — with a sorting game and the independent-domain scenario.

items.title: Cheat sheet: evidence
items.body:
Keep this handy while you write.

**The five domains**
- Mobility
- Cognition
- Communication
- Self-care and domestic ADL
- Social interaction

**Only what relates to the disability.** If something has no functional implication, leave it out. Tailor the report to the participant.

**Name every source.** Combine formal documentation, assessment results, reported information and functional observations (include these where possible).

**Every assessment has a purpose.** Refer to each one by name throughout the report.

**Where to find assessments:** the NDIS website (search for types of disability evidence), the Resource Hub, and sites such as Q Global.

items.title: Walkthrough: Recommendations that link up
items.body: Link every support to a need, to reasonable and necessary, and to a goal. Write the risk of no support honestly — then spot the mistakes that weaken a report.

sections.title: How we build it in the portal

items.title: Live tour: build an FCA in the portal
items.body: The walkthrough takes you through the real screens — Resource Hub › Templates › **Functional Capacity Assessment (FCA)** › Start a document — and you click each step yourself. Use a practice or test record if your supervisor has one.

items.title: Walkthrough: Timing and supervisor review
items.body: How long a report takes, when to send it, and why your first reports go to your clinical supervisor first.

items.title: Who to contact
items.body: Contact IT for portal or template problems, and for further support with assessments and information.

items.title: Start a practice template
items.body:
In the portal, open the Resource Hub › Templates and select **Functional Capacity Assessment (FCA)**. Use **Start a document** with a practice or test record if your supervisor has one. Do not use a real client without a reason to.

Then:

- Download the template.
- Decide which sections you would remove or add for a participant with a physical disability.
- Note which assessments you would use and why.

Bring your notes to your next supervision.

items.title: Knowledge check
items.body: Seven questions across the whole induction. You need 80% to pass, and you can retry.

questions.question: A participant has a physical disability and no cognitive or intellectual disability. Which domains will you most likely focus on?
options: Cognition and communication
Mobility, self-care and domestic ADL
Social interaction only

questions.question: A participant is independent in communication. What should you do?
options: Leave communication out
Describe difficulties that are not there
Say they are independent, and highlight any weaknesses and support needs that remain

questions.question: You found a piece of information with no functional impact on the disability. What do you do?
options: Include it for completeness
Put it in the appendix
Leave it out

questions.question: How should you use an assessment in the report?
options: Include it once at the end
Name it and refer back to it throughout, where it has a clear purpose
Use as many as possible

questions.question: How should each recommended support be written?
options: Linked to a reasonable and necessary need and to a participant goal
As a list of items with no explanation
Linked to the most expensive option

questions.question: How do you write the risk of a support not being provided?
options: Paint the worst case, even if the evidence does not show it
Describe what could realistically happen, based on the evidence, as a potential outcome
Leave it out to keep the report short

questions.question: It is your second FCA report. Your supervisor is away and the deadline is close. What do you do?
options: Send it, since deadlines come first
Send it only if it is under 8 weeks
Arrange the supervisor review before it is sent

items.title: Sign-off
items.body: Confirm you have read this induction and understand how we write FCA reports.
items.ack_statement: I have read the induction on writing an FCA report. I will keep reports accurate, sourced, consistent and limited to information related to the participant's disability. I will link each recommendation to a reasonable and necessary need and a goal. I will not invent or exaggerate information. I will have my clinical supervisor review my reports before they are sent until my supervisor confirms I can submit them on my own.

walkthroughs.title: Paint the picture
walkthroughs.description: What an FCA is for, the five domains, and honest reporting.

steps.title: What an FCA report is for
steps.body:
A functional capacity assessment (FCA) is one of the main reports an OT writes under the NDIS.

Your job is to show the planner that the participant has an NDIS-recognised disability and that it reduces their independence. **That is why they need support.**

steps.title: Five NDIS domains

image.alt: The participant at the centre of five NDIS domains.

steps.body:
The report looks at how the participant functions across the main NDIS domains:
• Mobility
• Cognition
• Communication
• Self-care and domestic ADL
• Social interaction

steps.title: Quick check: the job of the report

quiz.question: What does your FCA report need to show the planner?
options: That the participant has an NDIS-recognised disability that reduces their independence in these domains
Every assessment you know how to run
The most supports the participant could possibly receive
quiz.explain: That is why they need support — and it is the thread the whole report follows.

steps.title: Paint a picture of daily life

image.alt: A vague statement next to a sourced report built from named sources and functional observations.

steps.body:
The planner will most likely never meet the participant. **Your report is all they have.**

Our reports tell the story of what the participant is like and what their day-to-day life looks like. Use sourced detail and functional observations. Do not use vague or general statements.

quiz.question: Which kind of statement helps the planner picture the participant?
options: A general statement that the participant finds things hard
Sourced detail and functional observations of their day-to-day life
A long list of diagnoses with no description
quiz.explain: The planner should finish reading and understand how this person presents.

steps.title: Honest reporting

image.alt: Say when a participant is independent, then show remaining needs; never invent or exaggerate.

steps.body:
**Do not invent or exaggerate information.**

If a participant is independent in a domain, say so. Then highlight the weaknesses and support needs that remain in that domain.

A report the planner can trust is more useful to the participant than a dramatic one.

quiz.question: Your made-up participant, Sam, has a physical disability. Sam is independent with communication and manages most social activities. What do you do?
options: Leave communication and social interaction out of the report
State that Sam is independent in these domains, then note any remaining weaknesses or support needs, with the source for each
Describe some difficulties to strengthen the case
quiz.explain: Do not overstate difficulties to strengthen the case. Honest reporting is what makes the rest of the report believable.

steps.title: Picture painted
steps.body:
**Five domains, sourced detail, honest reporting.**

Back in your induction, next up: building the evidence.

walkthroughs.title: Build the evidence
walkthroughs.description: Tailor to the disability, name your sources, choose assessments with a purpose.

steps.title: Include only what relates to the disability

image.alt: A physical disability centres mobility and ADLs; a cognitive or intellectual disability may not affect mobility.

steps.body:
Only include information that relates to the participant's disability and its functional impact. If something has no functional implication, leave it out.

With a **physical disability** you will most likely focus on mobility, self-care and domestic ADL. You would still state any impact on cognition, communication or social interaction, but this is unlikely unless there is also a neurodevelopmental or intellectual disability.

With a mainly **cognitive or intellectual disability**, mobility may not be affected, so do not spend long on it.

quiz.question: Your participant has a mainly intellectual disability and walks without difficulty. How much of the report goes on mobility?
options: As much as every other domain, to be thorough
Little — mobility may not be affected, so do not spend long on it
None, and do not mention mobility at all
quiz.explain: Tailor the report to the participant: spend your words where the disability has a functional impact.

quiz.question: You found a piece of information with no functional implication for the disability. What do you do?
options: Include it for completeness
Leave it out
Move it to the end
quiz.explain: If something has no functional implication, leave it out.

steps.title: Name your sources

image.alt: Four sources feeding the report: formal documentation, assessment results, reported information, functional observations.

steps.body:
Name the source of each piece of information. Combine:
• Formal documentation
• Assessment results
• Reported information
• Functional observations (include these where possible)

steps.title: Every assessment has a purpose

image.alt: Match each assessment to a purpose, and where to find them.

steps.body:
Choose assessments based on the disability and on what you need to show the planner. Refer to each assessment **by name** throughout the report. Do not use an assessment without a purpose.

In your first reports, your clinical supervisor will go through with you which ones suit each participant.

quiz.question: The participant has cognitive difficulties. What do your assessments need to include?
options: Specific cognitive assessments
A focus on carer burden
As many assessments as possible
quiz.explain: Cognitive difficulties call for specific cognitive assessments.

quiz.question: The participant's informal carer is burning out. Where should your assessment focus?
options: Mobility
Carer burden
Nowhere — it is not about the participant
quiz.explain: Informal carer burnout calls for a focus on carer burden.

steps.title: Where to find assessments
steps.body:
Many standardised assessments can be used, depending on the disability.

The **NDIS website** lists the general assessments the NDIS typically expects to see. Search for types of disability evidence.

Many assessment PDFs are in the **Resource Hub**. Others are accessed through sites such as **Q Global**. All clinicians have access to Q Global.

steps.title: Evidence built
steps.body:
**Only what relates to the disability, every source named, every assessment with a purpose.**

The cheat sheet in your induction keeps this to hand. Next: recommendations and risk.

walkthroughs.title: Recommendations that link up
walkthroughs.description: Need, reasonable and necessary, goal — the risk of no support, and mistakes to avoid.

steps.title: Write recommendations that link up

image.alt: A support linked to its need, to reasonable and necessary, and to a goal, plus the risk if not provided.

steps.body:
For each recommended support, show:
• the need it responds to
• why it is reasonable and necessary
• the participant goal it relates to

The template gives you the format for this. It takes more time, but it shows the planner you have thought through each recommendation.

quiz.question: Which recommendation is written the way the template asks?
options: A list of supports with no explanation
Each support linked to the need it responds to, why it is reasonable and necessary, and the goal it relates to
Each support linked to the most expensive option
quiz.explain: This shows the planner how each support meets reasonable and necessary criteria.

steps.title: State the risk of no support

image.alt: Do: evidence-based, realistic, a potential outcome. Don't: the invented worst case.

steps.body:
Also state what could happen if a recommended support is not provided. This does not say it will happen. It shows the **potential outcome**.

You are not making anything up. Describe what could realistically happen for this participant, based on the evidence you have gathered. Remember the planner has never met them.

If you are unsure how to word a risk, talk it through with your supervisor.

steps.title: Scenario: the risk of no support

quiz.question: Your made-up participant, Alex, lives with an intellectual disability and has limited support at home. Alex's carer is close to burnout. How do you write the risk?
options: Describe the worst outcome you can imagine, to make the case strong
Describe what could realistically happen if the support is not funded, using your sources, and make clear it is a potential outcome
Leave the risk out — it is only a possibility
quiz.explain: For example, the carer may no longer be able to continue and Alex's daily routines may break down. Do not add outcomes the evidence does not support.

steps.title: Mistakes to avoid

image.alt: Six mistakes to avoid in an FCA report.

steps.body:
• Inconsistent information across the report
• Repeating information, which makes a long report hard to read
• Including information with no link to the disability
• Using an assessment and then not referring back to it
• Not naming where information came from
• Inventing or exaggerating information

Keep it concise and straight to the point.

quiz.question: Your draft runs a standardised assessment in the method section, but the results are never mentioned again. What is wrong?
options: Nothing — it was listed
The assessment is never referred back to
It should have been in the appendix only
quiz.explain: Refer to each assessment by name throughout the report. Do not use an assessment without a purpose.

quiz.question: The same background paragraph appears in three sections of your draft. What is the problem?
options: Repetition makes a long report hard to read
It is fine — repetition shows consistency
It needs a fourth copy in the summary
quiz.explain: Keep it concise and straight to the point.

steps.title: Recommendations linked
steps.body:
**Need → reasonable and necessary → goal**, plus an honest risk of no support.

Next: building the report in the portal.

walkthroughs.title: Build an FCA in the portal
walkthroughs.description: A live tour: Templates › Functional Capacity Assessment (FCA) › Start a document › Content.

steps.title: From start to download
steps.body:
You will click each step yourself:

**Resource Hub › Templates › Functional Capacity Assessment (FCA) › Start a document**

Then pick the client, edit the template in the portal, and download it to your laptop. Use a practice or test record if your supervisor has one.

steps.title: Open Templates

image.alt: The Templates screen with the FCA card highlighted.

steps.body: In the Resource Hub, select **Templates**.

steps.title: Start an FCA

image.alt: The FCA card's Start a document button.

steps.body: On the **Functional Capacity Assessment (FCA)** card, select **Start a document**.

steps.title: Find the client

image.alt: The New FCA dialog with a participant search box.

steps.body: Enter the client's **name or NDIS number**, then pick them from the list. The portal creates a pre-populated template.

steps.title: Create it

image.alt: The Create button in the New FCA dialog.

steps.body: Select **Create**.

steps.title: Open the Content step
steps.body: Select **Content** to see the report's sections.

steps.title: Add or remove sections

image.alt: Report contents: remove a section with its cross, reorder by dragging, add with + Add a section.

steps.body: Add or remove sections to suit the disability and your recommendations. The ✕ removes a section, and **+ Add a section** adds one. If a useful section is missing, add it.

steps.title: Download it

image.alt: The Download Word and Download PDF buttons.

steps.body: Edit the template in the portal, then **download it to your laptop**. You can keep editing the document after you download it.

steps.title: Template built
steps.body:
**Templates › FCA › Start a document → client → Content → download.**

Next in your induction: timing and supervisor review.

walkthroughs.title: Timing and supervisor review
walkthroughs.description: When to send, how long it takes, and why early reports are reviewed first.

steps.title: Timing: a guide, not a stopwatch

image.alt: Send within about 4 to 8 weeks of the assessment starting; allow about 5 to 10 hours to write.

steps.body:
Aim to send reports within **4 to 8 weeks** of the start of the assessment. This is a guide. It depends on access to the client and how quickly assessments are completed. Aiming for it stops reports piling up.

If there is a deadline, we honour it. Reports are prioritised accordingly.

A report usually takes about **5 to 10 hours** to write, and more if it is complex. Early on it will take longer, and your clinical supervisor will help you decide how many hours to allow.

quiz.question: A referrer has set a deadline earlier than the usual 4 to 8 weeks. What happens?
options: We honour the deadline and prioritise the report
The 4 to 8 week guide wins
The report waits until the assessments are all perfect
quiz.explain: If there is a deadline, we honour it. Reports are prioritised accordingly.

steps.title: What every report must be
steps.body:
Opal's FCA writing procedure says reports must be:

**accurate · sourced · consistent · limited to disability-related information · reviewed before sending**

steps.title: Supervisor review

image.alt: Early reports each reviewed by the supervisor; independent submission once the supervisor is confident.

steps.body:
For your first few reports, your clinical supervisor must review each one and give you feedback before it is sent.

Once your supervisor is confident in your reports, you can submit them on your own. This is likely to be after about five reports have gone well. **Your supervisor decides when.**

Until then, do not send a report without your supervisor's review.

quiz.question: It is your second FCA report. Your supervisor is away and the deadline is close. What do you do?
options: Send it, since deadlines come first
Arrange the supervisor review before it is sent
Ask a colleague to send it for you
quiz.explain: Early reports must be reviewed by your clinical supervisor before they are sent.

steps.title: Ready to write
steps.body:
**4 to 8 weeks as a guide, deadlines honoured, supervisor review first.**

Back in your induction: who to contact, a practice template, the knowledge check and sign-off.

policy.name: FCA report writing procedure (name to be confirmed)
policy.summary: Reports must be accurate, sourced, consistent, limited to information related to the disability, and reviewed before sending.

openQuestions: What is the official name of the FCA report writing policy or procedure, and is the suggested name correct?

Is the supervisor review step (every report reviewed for the first few, then independent sign-off once the supervisor is confident, about five reports) final? How long should supervisor review take? (Related to D16, not decided.)
Which FCA template version is current, and who has authority to release finished reports? (D18 not decided.)
Is there an Opal Way value or practice point to add? None was discussed.
Should a practice or test client record be provided for the practical task?
